**"The Weight of Something and Nothing"**

The first thing I noticed about the old bookstore was the smell—damp paper, ink long dried, the faintest trace of tobacco lingering in the corners like a ghost. It was tucked between a laundromat and a boarded-up diner, its window display crooked with dust and half-faded memories. The sign above the door read *Hollow’s End* in peeling gold letters, the "W" missing entirely, as if the past had fallen asleep mid-title and forgot to wake up.

I pushed the door open and the hinges groaned like an old man stretching after a nap. Inside, the shelves sagged under the weight of books that hadn’t been moved in decades. The air was thick, slow, the kind of quiet that settles into your bones after you’ve stood too long in a museum of forgotten things.

A man sat behind the counter, his back to me, paging through a ledger with the care of someone reading a sacred text. His shoulders were broad, his hair silver at the temples, but his hands—ah, his hands were the hands of a younger man, fingers long and deft, making the ledger’s leather spine creak under his touch.

“You’re late,” he said without turning around.

I blinked. “Late for what?”

He finally swiveled in his chair, and I saw his face—a face that had worn a hundred faces before this one, each one softer, then harder, then softer again, like waves smoothing a stone. His eyes were the color of storm clouds over a drowned city. “For the last story,” he said. “Sit down.”

I hesitated. The store felt like a place where stories went to die, not be told. “I don’t even know if I believe in stories anymore.”

He smiled, just a little. “That’s the problem with you modern ones. You think belief is a switch—on or off. But stories aren’t like that. They’re more like the tide. They come in whether you ask them or not.”

I pulled up a stool, and the wood groaned under my weight. The stool’s legs were uneven; one side shorter than the others. I had the sudden, irrational fear that if I shifted even slightly, the whole thing would collapse into splinters.

“What do you mean, the *last* story?” I asked.

The man—*Hollow*, I realized, because that must be his name—leaned back in his chair. The leather creaked like a warning. “Every bookstore has a last book. Every town has a last street. Every person has a last thing they say before they forget how to speak. This place is no different.” He tapped the ledger with one finger. “I’ve been waiting for you to arrive.”

A chill ran down my arms. “Waiting for me? How long have you been here?”

“Longer than you’ve been alive.” He flipped the ledger shut. The sound was like a gunshot in the quiet. “But that doesn’t matter. What matters is that you’re here now.”

I should have left. I should have walked out that crooked door and never looked back. But something in his voice—the way it wrapped around my ribs and squeezed—made it impossible to move.

“Tell me the last story,” I said.

Hollow’s lips curled into a smile that didn’t reach his eyes. “Sit closer.”

I did.

----------------

The story wasn’t about heroes or villains or grand quests. It was about a man who collected silence the way other men collect stamps or coins. He lived in a house where the walls were lined with jars, each one holding a different kind of quiet: the silence of a child who’d just learned to walk; the silence of a dog just before its leash is tightened; the silence of a lover’s last breath.

One day, the man woke up and realized his jars were empty.

Not because the silence had been broken, but because it had been *used up*. Every quiet moment he’d ever stolen, every pause he’d hoarded like a miser—it had all been spent somewhere else. Someone else had been listening when he thought no one could hear.

He spent the rest of his life searching for the silence he’d wasted, but he never found it. All he found were echoes.

----------------

I sat in that creaking chair, staring at Hollow’s hands. They were doing the strangest thing—flipping through the pages of the ledger, but the ink wasn’t black. It was the color of dried blood.

“Is that a real ledger?” I asked.

“Oh yes,” he said. “But it’s not for sales. It’s for absences. Every time someone forgets a story, every time a name fades from memory, every time a door stays shut just one second too long—it goes in here.” He tapped the page. “See this? *Your name.* Written in pencil. It’s the faintest ink in the book.”

My throat went dry. “That’s not possible.”

“Isn’t it?” He closed the ledger. “You’ve forgotten so much already. Your first dog. The name of your first love. The last time you laughed so hard you cried.” His voice dropped to a whisper. “Tell me, do you even remember your *last* word before you walked into this shop today?”

I opened my mouth. Nothing came out.

Hollow stood. The chair scraped back with a sound like fingernails on a chalkboard. “The thing about last stories,” he said, “is that they’re always waiting. Like a train that leaves in ten minutes but never arrives.” He walked around the counter, his boots scuffing against the floorboards. “You can stay, if you like. I’ll never ask for rent. But someday, you’ll have to leave, and when you do, you’ll take the silence with you. And I’d advise against that.”

I wanted to ask him what would happen if I did. I wanted to ask him if he was real. I wanted to ask him how long he’d been waiting in that dusty shop, collecting stories like a miser until the last one was gone.

But I didn’t.

Because by the time I opened my mouth again, the door was already swinging shut behind me, and the sign above it read *Hollow* in letters that faded into nothing.

And I realized—I didn’t even remember walking out.
